description: A team where you should always expect the unexpected
summary:
TerraSync is a web app with no build step that finds the places on Earth most like sites on Mars and the Moon. For Mars, it compares Earth and Mars sites across nine areas: geology, terrain, temperature, dust and wind, water and ice, habitability, what lies below the surface, surface processes, and operations. Slopes are compared using fixed physical scales and full slope distributions. Each pair gets a clear score, a list of where the analogy holds and where it breaks, and what the Earth site could be used to test. The terrain behind it is real: elevation, slope and shadow maps from HiRISE stereo models and MOLA, plus ESA WorldCover land-cover data for Earth. For the Moon, the “Lunar Light” section ranks Earth places by how closely their low-Sun light and shadows match the lunar south pole, using LOLA and Copernicus elevation data. An Education section teaches the ideas through story cards and a quiz game.

This matters because testing rovers, landing systems and astronaut training on Mars or the Moon is very expensive. Picking the right Earth stand-in, and knowing exactly where it falls short, makes testing cheaper and safer. Each value is marked as measured or synthetic, and pressure, radiation and gravity are listed as limits rather than scored, so users know how far to trust each result.
details:
What it does and how it works

TerraSync is a web app that finds the places on Earth that best match landing and base sites on Mars and the Moon. It also explains why each place matches and where the match falls short. You start by choosing one of three sections: Mars, Moon or Education.

Mars: Find a Twin and Compare. You pick a place on Mars and get a ranked list of Earth places. Each pair is scored across nine areas: geology, terrain, temperature, dust and wind, water and ice, habitability, what lies below the surface, surface processes, and operations.

  • Numbers are compared on fixed physical scales. This means a pair’s score stays the same when sites are added or removed. Values that vary over a very wide range use a log scale.
  • Slopes are compared as whole distributions: we measure how much two slope histograms (in 1° steps) overlap, instead of comparing only the average slope.
  • Lists and tags are compared by how many items they share.
  • A pair that shares less than a third of the nine areas is shown as “Limited data” and is not scored.
  • Pressure, radiation and gravity cannot be copied on Earth. They are shown as limits of the match and are not scored.
  • The Amazon rainforest is included as a test case that should not match. It checks that the method can tell a real analog from a bad one.

The Compare page puts one Earth place next to one Mars place. It shows the score, where they match, where they differ, and what the Earth place could be used to test.

Measured Mars terrain. We worked with two HiRISE 3D terrain maps from east of Jezero crater and kept their original ~2 m detail. We then averaged them to 30 m, counting only valid data and filling no gaps. From these we calculated:

  • slope, slope direction, local height range and surface roughness
  • light and shadow for 24 Sun positions (3 heights × 8 directions), using ray-traced cast shadows plus faces turned away from the Sun
  • regional context from MOLA laser altimeter data

Moon: Lunar Light. This section ranks Earth places by how closely their light and shadow match the lunar south pole. The score is 60% shadow similarity plus 40% time with the Sun low in the sky. We used LOLA elevation data for the south pole (Shackleton, de Gerlache, Shoemaker, Faustini, Haworth, Malapert and others). For Earth we used Copernicus GLO-30 elevation data for Haughton Crater, the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Peary Land, Svalbard, Askja, Sudbury, Ries, Meteor Crater, Mauna Kea and more. We modeled the Sun 1–7° above the horizon from 12 directions, with shadows up to 20 km long and the curvature of each body taken into account.

Earth land cover. ESA WorldCover 10 m data gives measured plant cover around the Earth sites. Vegetation is a key reason an Earth place can fail as a Mars stand-in.

Education. Six story cards that flip over follow a rookie learning what makes a good analog, with titles like “The beach mistake” and “The land of long shadows”. They end with a six-round quiz game, “Analog or Not?”, with scores and ranks.

Benefits

  • Cheaper, safer testing: it helps teams pick the right Earth place to test rovers, landing systems, lighting for solar power and navigation, and astronaut training before going to Mars or the Moon.
  • Clear about what’s missing: every match lists where it breaks, so an Earth site is never treated as a perfect copy.
  • Honest data: every field is marked as measured or synthetic, so users know how far to trust each result.
  • Easy to use: it runs in any browser with no install, account or backend, and stores no data.
  • Reproducible: Python pipelines rebuild every data file, and source files are recorded with SHA256 checksums.

Intended impact

We want to make picking analog sites more open, measurable and repeatable. Right now it often relies on expert judgment and habit. Mission planners, researchers and students can see why a place is or isn’t a good stand-in. The Moon section focuses on the lunar south pole, which is the target of upcoming Artemis missions, where extreme low-Sun lighting is one of the hardest conditions to copy on Earth. The Education section helps students understand how planetary analogs and mission planning work.

Tools, languages and software

  • Front end: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules), with no frameworks, build step or dependencies. All charts (maps, radar charts, heatmaps, scatter plots, dials, slope distributions) are hand-written SVG. It includes its own CSV parser and URL-based page routing.
  • Data processing: Python with NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Numba (for fast shadow ray-tracing) and Matplotlib. Jupyter notebooks were used for cleaning and analysis.
  • Data: NASA MRO HiRISE 3D terrain maps and MGS MOLA (from the PDS Geosciences Node), LRO LOLA for the lunar south pole, Copernicus GLO-30 elevation (streamed from its public AWS bucket), ESA WorldCover, and Natural Earth coastlines.
  • Hardware: [fill in, e.g., team laptops; no special hardware was needed]
  • If your team used AI tools during development, Space Apps asks you to disclose that. Add it here if it applies.

How it’s creative

  • Two-way matches: every match explains where the analogy holds and where it breaks, instead of giving just one score.
  • Matching light, not just ground: the Moon section compares how light and shadow behave, not only elevation or rock type. This is the key issue at the lunar south pole.
  • Slope as a shape: comparing whole slope distributions shows how drivable a terrain really is, which an average slope hides.
  • A built-in test case: the Amazon “non-analog” checks that the method can tell analogs apart from non-analogs.
  • Learning through play: a story told with flip cards and a quiz turns a niche science topic into something students can explore.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific honesty: we filled no gaps and did no smoothing. Different elevation reference levels (Mars 2000 vs. the GMM3 areoid) are kept separate and never merged, the two HiRISE patches are never stitched together, and shadow results that can’t be resolved are marked as unknown, not as lit. Sun angles are clearly labeled as hypothetical.
  • Data limits: we track per field whether each value is measured or synthetic. Pairs with too little shared data are not scored.
  • Stable scoring: fixed physical scales mean results don’t change when the dataset grows.
  • Things Earth can’t copy: pressure, radiation and gravity are stated openly instead of hidden in a score.
  • Accessibility: the app has screen-reader labels and respects users’ “reduce motion” settings.
  • Privacy and reach: there’s no login, tracking or server, so it runs anywhere.
  • Reproducibility: others can rebuild every result with the included pipelines and settings files
